## Scope

This review covers the literature on catalysts for carbon dioxide hydrogenation, that is, the reaction of carbon dioxide with hydrogen over a solid catalyst to give reduced carbon products, with methanol chief among them in the literature reviewed. The evidence base consists of 109 papers published over the last 12 years. A paper is included in the review if it reports a catalyst tested for this reaction with measured activity or selectivity, presented in a form that allows the test conditions to be recovered; papers that report a catalyst for the reverse reaction, or for the hydrogenation of carbon monoxide alone, fall outside the scope, because the water formed from carbon dioxide changes both the catalyst surface and the equilibrium position, meaning that results from the carbon monoxide reaction do not transfer without that correction.

It is worth emphasising that the scope is set by the reaction, rather than by the catalyst family. Copper-based catalysts dominate the base, just as they dominate the field, but oxide catalysts, noble-metal catalysts and carbide systems are all included on the same terms, so that the established results presented below reflect what the whole literature supports, and not merely what its largest family supports. Test conditions are treated as part of the evidence wherever they are reported: temperature, pressure, feed composition and space velocity are recorded alongside each result, because the disagreements section turns on them. Where a paper omits a condition that is needed for comparison, the result is carried as reported and flagged as incomparable, rather than being silently aligned with the others. The review is a reading of published measurements: it does not re-measure any catalyst, and its claims stand at the scope that the published record supports.

## Established results

Copper dispersed on zinc oxide, usually with alumina as a structural component, is the established catalyst system for methanol formation from carbon dioxide and hydrogen, and the published record supports it at a depth that no rival system currently matches. The working picture that the literature converges on has the reaction proceeding at the interface between the copper surface and the oxide: the oxide and the interface adsorb and activate carbon dioxide, the copper supplies dissociated hydrogen, and zinc species that migrate onto the copper under reaction conditions are implicated in the active site by several independent lines of evidence. The preparation method also matters, at a level the record establishes beyond dispute: catalysts prepared by co-precipitation, with the copper and zinc intimately mixed before reduction, outperform impregnated preparations of the same nominal composition, and the difference is attributed to the dispersion and interface area that the preparation creates.

Water represents the second established result. The reaction produces water, water competes for the very sites that the reaction needs, and exposure to water sinters copper; consequently, rates fall and selectivity shifts as the water partial pressure rises, and every durable result in the record is reported against that constraint. Temperature divides the products: methanol formation is favoured at lower temperatures, where equilibrium allows it but kinetics are slow, whereas the reverse water-gas shift reaction, which gives carbon monoxide, takes a growing share as the temperature rises. Promoters modify this picture at the margins rather than overturning it: zirconia as a support or promoter is repeatedly associated with improved stability and methanol selectivity, and alkali and other additives shift activity in directions that depend on loading. Overall, supports, promoters and preparation are the established levers, while the reaction network and the water constraint form the established frame within which they operate.

## Disagreements

Reports conflict on methanol selectivity at a given conversion, and, along with it, on the ranking of catalyst formulations that the selectivity figures imply. One group reports a formulation as a clear advance on the copper-zinc oxide benchmark, while another group, testing a closely similar formulation, finds it at or below the benchmark. The conflict is identified here as a conflict about selectivity at matched conversion, because that is the quantity on which the claims are made and the quantity that the record does not settle.

On weighing the two sides, the review concludes that the conflict follows the test conditions more than it follows the catalysts themselves. Selectivity to methanol falls as conversion rises along any one catalyst, because the product distribution shifts as products accumulate and water builds up; two reports at different conversions are therefore not measuring the same point, and a formulation compared against a benchmark at unmatched conversion can be made to look either better or worse purely by the choice of operating point. Feed composition also differs across the conflicting reports, in particular the share of carbon monoxide in the feed, which changes both the water formed and the surface state; space velocity differs as well, which moves conversion independently of the catalyst; and several reports state selectivity on a carbon basis that excludes carbon monoxide while others include it, so that the same experiment would print two different selectivity figures under the two conventions. Where the conditions are brought closest together — comparable conversion, comparable feed, and the same selectivity convention — the disagreement narrows to the size of the claimed advances, and the ranking of the leading formulations is not established by the present record. The limited preference the review reaches is for reports that state selectivity at a stated conversion on a stated basis: their claims can be checked, whereas the unchecked remainder cannot.

## Gaps

The measurement that nobody reports is catalyst stability, measured in a way that allows comparison. Papers report activity and selectivity from short tests, commonly at the start of operation; long runs are rare, and where a catalyst is held on stream, the report seldom gives the rate of deactivation as a measured quantity with the conditions of the run — the water partial pressure above all — stated beside it. Deactivation is the property that decides whether a catalyst survives contact with the water that this reaction necessarily makes, and it is the property that the record leaves unmeasured in comparable form. As a result, a formulation can lead the literature on activity and selectivity while its standing on the property that governs its working life remains unknown, and the present record provides no basis for ranking catalysts on lifetime at all.

This gap propagates through the rest of the review. Because deactivation is not reported on a common basis, the established results rest disproportionately on initial performance; the disagreements cannot be closed by appeal to long-run behaviour; and a reader who needs to choose a catalyst for sustained operation finds the literature richest exactly where the decision needs it least. Secondary gaps follow the same pattern: carbon balances are not always closed in print, so selectivity figures cannot always be audited, and the state of the catalyst after reaction is characterised less often than the state before it. The review closes on the primary gap: until deactivation under stated conditions is measured and reported as routinely as initial activity, comparisons in this field will continue to compare beginnings.
